data.content_ref: inline:The target's mechanism claims to avoid induction via the chess-gambit analogy: preferring a gambit 'that has worked before' is said to avoid induction by 'refusing to assign higher probability to the future success of the gambit.' But the analogy's own stated justification is that the gambit 'offers the fastest route to checkmate or refutation.' This is a predictive claim about the gambit's future efficacy—derived from its having 'worked before.' Claiming a past-surviving gambit will offer the fastest future resolution is no less inductive than claiming it will win; both treat past performance as evidence about future performance. The analogy does not eliminate induction but merely relocates it from 'probability of success' to 'speed of resolution,' smuggling in the very inference it purports to avoid.
